strengths: The layered ray-intersection/point-map representation is a clear and useful idea: it extends depth/point-map prediction from the first visible surface to ordered intersections along each camera ray, giving a compact, camera-aligned formulation for occluded geometry.

The paper addresses both object-level and scene-level settings with a unified formulation, and the reported results are promising: on GSO it is competitive with TRELLIS under canonical alignment and stronger under view-aligned evaluation, while using substantially fewer parameters and faster inference.
The ray stopping index is a sensible modeling choice for enforcing ordered valid layers, and the ablation against independent binary masks shows a large improvement in mask quality.

The data-generation pipeline is practically valuable, especially the discussion of cleaning Objaverse, room-splitting 3D-FRONT, and coordinating Blender/PyTorch3D to render layered intersections. Releasing this benchmark/pipeline could be useful to the community.
The limitations section is honest about important representational issues, including low density on surfaces parallel to rays and failure under severe occlusion.
weaknesses: The central claim of “complete” geometry reasoning is overstated. LaRI only predicts intersections along rays from the input camera, so it cannot densely represent surfaces not intersected well by those rays, surfaces parallel to the view direction, or geometry between sampled layers; Fig. 5 acknowledges this, but the main text repeatedly frames the method as complete geometry reconstruction.

The evaluation has fairness and interpretability issues. Object-level evaluation uses GT masks to remove invalid regions, which may not reflect deployment and can hide mask-prediction errors. View-aligned GT also naturally favors LaRI’s camera-coordinate output over generative baselines whose coordinate frame is not designed for that setting.

The scene-level comparison is less convincing than the object-level one. Depth/point-map baselines do not attempt unseen geometry, so “overall” comparisons are hard to interpret; CUT3R is run with only five virtual poses and is mostly a reference rather than a tuned baseline. The identical overall scores for Ours and Ours* despite different visible/unseen sampling also need clearer explanation.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for full confidence. The authors promise to release data/scripts, but the manuscript does not provide enough detail to reproduce the filtering thresholds, ray-layer rendering procedure, training schedule, total epochs, loss weighting, or exact evaluation settings such as ICP search parameters.

Some claims rely on data-scale comparisons that may be misleading: LaRI uses strong pretrained weights from MoGe/DINOv2, so statements such as achieving results with only 4% of TRELLIS training data do not fully account for pretraining data and supervision inherited from the backbone.

The data construction makes strong assumptions that may bias the learned task. Filtering Objaverse objects by assuming most valid intersections occur in the first two layers may remove precisely the complex multi-layer cases that the method is meant to handle.

Presentation is generally clear, but there are notable technical/citation issues, e.g. ViT-Large is cited as [75] in the method where [75] is the SSIM paper, and some equations/descriptions are imprecise, such as describing the ground-truth stopping target as logits. These do not break the paper but reduce polish and confidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and useful problem: predicting occluded 3D geometry from a single image in a view-aligned representation that can cover both object-level and indoor scene-level settings.

The layered ray intersection representation is simple, intuitive, and computationally attractive. Casting multi-surface geometry along each camera ray as a dense 2D regression problem is a practical design that can reuse strong image backbones.

The authors make a real effort to build training data for a nonstandard target, combining Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, ScanNet++, Blender, and PyTorch3D, with some discussion of asset cleaning and coordinate alignment.

The experiments include several relevant baselines and ablations. The reported object-level view-aligned results and inference-time numbers suggest the method may be efficient and competitive in the specific camera-aligned setting.
The limitations section honestly notes important failure modes, including low point density for surfaces parallel to rays, difficulty under heavy occlusion, and limited dataset diversity.
weaknesses: The central claims of complete unseen geometry reasoning are overstated. From a single image, many occluded surfaces are inherently ambiguous, and the method is learning dataset priors rather than recovering complete geometry. The paper does not sufficiently qualify this distinction in the main claims.

Originality is moderate. The method is closely related to layered depth images/depth peeling and dense point-map prediction; the main novelty is adapting this representation to learned single-view occluded geometry prediction rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle.

The evaluation has important soundness concerns. In canonical object coordinates, the method is slightly worse than TRELLIS, while the main win comes from the view-aligned evaluation that strongly favors LaRI's output parameterization. This is a valid setting, but the paper presents it too broadly as superiority over generative methods.

Scene-level comparisons are not fully convincing. Most baselines only predict visible geometry, so comparing overall visible+unseen scores is not an apples-to-apples test of occluded geometry reasoning. CUT3R is included only in one iter-5 configuration, and stronger or better-tuned amodal/scene-completion baselines are missing.

The use of scale-shift alignment and GT masks during evaluation weakens claims about real-world applicability and metric reconstruction. The paper should report performance without privileged masks or with predicted masks fully integrated into evaluation, including mask errors' effect on final geometry.

There is a possible inconsistency in efficiency reporting: the method uses separate ViT-Large backbones for LaRI regression and ray stopping index prediction, but Table 5 appears to report around one model's parameter count and inference time. If both networks are required, the efficiency advantage may be substantially smaller.

Ablations are limited. There is no clear ablation of the layered representation against simpler multi-depth/depth-completion variants, no analysis of how much performance comes from pretraining versus the proposed representation, and limited study of uncertainty or multimodality for ambiguous occlusions.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper promises release of data and scripts, but many critical details are underspecified: exact filtering thresholds for Objaverse/3D-FRONT, total training schedule, loss normalization, rendering conventions, model-decoder details, random seeds, and full evaluation scripts/ICP parameters.

The limitations and ethics treatment is too thin. It does not discuss dataset licensing/privacy considerations for real scans, potential downstream risks in robotics/AR from hallucinated occluded geometry, or how users should detect failures when the deterministic prediction is confidently wrong.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful representation: layered ray intersections as depth-ordered point maps, plus a ray stopping index to recover valid layers. This is a natural extension of depth/point-map estimation and provides a convincing way to make unseen geometry prediction view-aligned and feed-forward.

The contribution is significant because it bridges object-level single-image reconstruction and scene-level occluded geometry reasoning under one formulation. The view-aligned output is practically valuable, especially compared with generative methods that need registration or produce canonical-coordinate shapes.

The empirical evidence is fairly strong. On GSO, LaRI is competitive with TRELLIS under canonical GT and stronger under view-aligned GT, while using much less training data and fewer parameters. The scene-level SCRREAM evaluation usefully separates visible, unseen, and overall regions, demonstrating a capability that standard depth and point-map baselines do not provide.

The paper includes relevant ablations: number of layers, pretraining source, efficiency, and the ray stopping index versus binary mask prediction. These experiments support the main design choices, especially the ordered stopping-index formulation.

Presentation is generally strong. The figures make the representation easy to understand, the method is simple enough to reproduce in principle, and the limitations section is honest about low density for surfaces parallel to rays, between-layer gaps, deterministic failure under severe occlusion, and limited data diversity.

Reproducibility is above average for a conference submission if the promised release is fulfilled: the paper describes datasets, sample counts, rendering pipeline, model architecture, training resolution, optimizer, batch size, and evaluation metrics/scripts. The proposed release of annotation/evaluation code would make the benchmark useful to the community.
weaknesses: The strongest claims about complete geometric reasoning should be interpreted cautiously. LaRI only models ray-surface intersections from the input camera rays, so surfaces not intersected by those rays, surfaces parallel to rays, and between-layer regions are inherently underrepresented. The paper acknowledges this, but the term “complete” can overstate what the representation guarantees.

The scene-level evaluation is somewhat narrow: SCRREAM testing uses only 460 selected frames with at least 30% unseen structure. This is a useful stress test, but it leaves uncertainty about robustness across broader indoor layouts, outdoor scenes, clutter, transparent/specular objects, and natural image distributions.

The data construction pipeline is central to the method but not fully stress-tested. Filtering Objaverse objects by assuming most clean objects have intersections mainly in the first two layers may bias the training set toward certain geometries and against legitimately complex shapes. More analysis of what is removed and how that affects generalization would strengthen the paper.

The comparison to generative baselines is informative but not perfectly balanced. LaRI is evaluated in a view-aligned regime that directly matches its output representation, while generative methods are not designed for that coordinate convention; conversely, the canonical GT comparison still requires ICP for LaRI. The paper explains this distinction, but the headline superiority depends on the chosen practical setting.

The scene-level quantitative results are mixed on visible surfaces: MoGe remains substantially better for visible reconstruction, and LaRI’s overall advantage comes from modeling unseen regions. This is acceptable given the paper’s goal, but it means LaRI is not yet a uniformly better geometric estimator.

Ethics and limitations are lightly treated. The work appears to have low direct ethical risk, but downstream use in robotics/AR could be safety-critical, and the paper would benefit from clearer discussion of failure detection, uncertainty, and dataset bias before deployment.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and useful formulation: predicting layered, view-aligned ray-surface intersection point maps plus a ray stopping index. This is a natural extension of depth/point-map prediction to occluded geometry and gives a unified feed-forward interface for object- and scene-level reconstruction.

The experimental coverage is fairly broad: object-level GSO evaluation, scene-level 3D-FRONT and SCRREAM evaluation, visible/unseen/overall metrics, ablations over layer count, pretraining, mask formulation, shared vs separate encoders, and efficiency comparisons.

The results support the main practical claim that LaRI can recover additional unseen surfaces in one feed-forward pass. On scene-level benchmarks it substantially improves unseen-region scores over the CUT3R reference and improves overall completeness relative to visible-only depth/point-map baselines.

The annotation pipeline and benchmark construction are valuable. The paper clearly explains the coordinate-convention and rendering challenges, and the datasets span synthetic object assets, synthetic indoor scenes, and real scanned indoor data.

The limitations and impact statement are reasonably honest, noting poor density for surfaces parallel to rays, ambiguity under limited observations, synthetic-domain gaps, and the need for safeguards in downstream deployment.
weaknesses: The central claim of complete unseen 3D reasoning is only partially supported because hidden geometry from a single image is highly ambiguous, yet the method is deterministic and trained with one target geometry. The paper does not model uncertainty, multimodality, or evaluate plausibility/diversity for genuinely ambiguous occlusions.

Comparisons for scene-level unseen geometry are limited. Most baselines are visible-surface depth/point-map methods that cannot predict unseen regions, so the overall metric partly measures task mismatch. Stronger or more carefully adapted baselines from single-view scene completion, DRDF/KYN-style ray querying, amodal depth, or multi-layer depth methods are mostly discussed but not evaluated.

The real-world quantitative evidence is narrow: SCRREAM has only 11 scenes and 460 selected frames, and ScanNet++ is used mainly for training/visualization because unseen regions are incomplete. This weakens claims about real-world generalization.

The evaluation uses scale-shift alignment and sometimes ICP/brute-force registration, which is reasonable for relative geometry but limits claims about metric or directly deployable 3D accuracy. The paper should more clearly separate relative-shape accuracy from metric reconstruction capability.

Reproducibility is not yet fully established. The paper says the data generation pipeline will be released, but exact splits, rendering scripts, filtering criteria, architecture details for the adapted decoders, and trained model/code availability are not specified enough for reliable independent reproduction.

Originality is moderate rather than high: layered depth images and multi-layer scene representations are longstanding, and the main novelty is adapting them into a supervised point-map prediction framework with a ray-stopping classifier and datasets. This is useful, but not a conceptual breakthrough.

Presentation is generally clear, but some important methodological details are easy to miss or underspecified, such as how predicted masks are used in all evaluations, how visible/unseen regions are separated for non-layered baselines, and whether the 3D-FRONT evaluation subset differs in distribution from training beyond non-overlap.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful problem: single-view reconstruction should reason about occluded geometry rather than only visible depth. The layered ray-intersection representation is simple, view-aligned, and potentially useful for downstream perception pipelines that consume image-aligned 3D points.

The manuscript provides a reasonably clear formulation with a separate ray-stopping-index prediction head, and the ordinal stopping-index idea is a sensible way to enforce contiguous valid layers along a ray.

The authors put effort into dataset construction across Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, ScanNet++, GSO, and SCRREAM, and they discuss several practical annotation issues such as coordinate convention mismatches and noisy internal geometry.

The reported efficiency is a positive aspect: inference is substantially faster than large object generative baselines such as TRELLIS/SPAR3D, and the method can produce layered outputs in one feed-forward pass.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially overstated. LaRI does not perform complete 3D reconstruction; it predicts only surfaces intersected by the input camera rays, and the paper itself notes low point density for surfaces parallel to rays or between layers. This is a fundamental representational limitation, not merely a post-processing issue.

Originality is limited. The method is essentially supervised layered depth/point-map regression inspired by LDIs, combined with a classification head for the last valid layer. The paper does not provide enough new modeling insight to justify the broad framing as a major advance in geometric reasoning.

The evaluation does not convincingly support the main claims. Scene-level comparisons are mostly against depth or point-map methods that cannot predict unseen surfaces by design, so improvements on overall visible+unseen metrics are partly baked into the task setup. The most relevant occluded-geometry methods are largely omitted or only represented by a weak CUT3R configuration with arbitrary noisy virtual poses.

The object-level evaluation is difficult to interpret. Canonical evaluation uses brute-force rotation plus ICP, while view-aligned evaluation strongly favors LaRI's output format. The paper claims faithfulness advantages over generative models, but this is supported mainly by selected qualitative examples and not by rigorous perceptual, semantic, or category-level analysis.

The method relies on fully supervised rendered layered geometry from custom pipelines, filtered datasets, and separate object/scene training. The resulting generalization claims are therefore weak, especially for real-world occluded geometry where ground truth is incomplete, domain gaps are acknowledged, and SCRREAM evaluation contains only 460 selected frames from 11 scenes.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the strength of the claims. The paper says the data generation pipeline will be released, but the custom filtering, rendering, pose conversion, train/eval splits, and baseline adaptations are central to the results and not specified in enough detail to reproduce independently from the manuscript alone.

Several experimental choices raise soundness concerns: the scene evaluation states that GT masks are used; the binary-mask baseline in Table 7 performs implausibly poorly and may be under-tuned; the number-of-layers ablation shows little scene benefit; and scale-shift alignment undermines claims about metric usefulness for robotics or AR/VR.

The limitations and ethics discussion are present but too mild. The paper acknowledges ambiguity and domain gap, but does not fully confront safety risks of hallucinated occluded geometry, uncertainty calibration, or failure modes in downstream planning settings.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: single-view reconstruction of both visible and occluded geometry. The layered ray-intersection formulation is simple, view-aligned, and practically useful compared with implicit/query-heavy scene completion methods.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this problem setting: object-level evaluation on GSO, scene-level evaluation on 3D-FRONT and SCRREAM, and training/annotation across Objaverse, 3D-FRONT, and ScanNet++. The paper reports visible, unseen, and overall scene metrics, which directly tests the claimed occluded-geometry capability.

Results are convincing overall. LaRI is competitive with TRELLIS under canonical object evaluation and stronger under view-aligned evaluation, while being much faster. On scene reconstruction, it substantially improves unseen-region metrics over CUT3R and improves overall reconstruction over depth/point-map baselines on 3D-FRONT, while remaining competitive on SCRREAM.

The ray-stopping index is a clean solution to enforcing ordered valid layers, and the ablation against independent binary mask prediction supports this design. Additional ablations on number of layers, pretraining, separate/shared encoders, per-layer accuracy, and point maps versus depth maps strengthen the technical story.

The data construction discussion is unusually concrete, including coordinate-system pitfalls, asset filtering, dataset statistics, and limitations of synthetic rendering. The limitations and impact statements are appropriate and do not overclaim certainty in ambiguous occluded regions.
weaknesses: Originality is solid but not transformative: the representation is closely related to layered depth images and multi-layer depth ideas, with the main novelty being a supervised modern point-map formulation plus ray-stopping prediction and dataset construction. This is useful, but conceptually incremental rather than a new reconstruction paradigm.

The scene-level comparisons are somewhat incomplete. The paper excludes several occluded-geometry methods because they require masks, poses, or iterative queries, but the resulting comparison mostly pits LaRI against methods not designed to predict unseen surfaces. CUT3R is included only with a specific five-virtual-pose setup, and stronger or better-tuned amodal/scene-completion baselines would make the evidence more definitive.

The evaluation protocol has some ambiguity. The manuscript states that GT masks are used for scene evaluation, but it is not fully clear how predicted ray-stopping masks affect final point-cloud metrics versus only region partitioning. Since mask prediction quality is moderate (mIoU around 0.55), clearer separation between oracle-mask and predicted-mask reconstruction would be important for reproducibility and interpretation.

The method is fully supervised and depends on expensive rendering/annotation pipelines and complete 3D assets/scans. Generalization beyond the curated indoor/object domains remains only partially established; outdoor scenes and more diverse real-world clutter are deferred to future work.

The model is still large when both point-map and index networks are used (about 620M parameters), and the separate-encoder design doubles much of the computation. The efficiency claim is convincing relative to large generative methods, but less compelling relative to the strongest feed-forward depth/geometry models such as MoGe.

Some presentation details need polish: there are minor citation/typographical issues, the architecture description is fairly high level, and exact release artifacts are promised rather than available in the manuscript. Reproducibility would benefit from more precise training schedules, preprocessing parameters, and annotation-code details.
